overview: This bill concerns China's voting power at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the international organization that lends to countries in financial trouble and in which each member's vote depends largely on its financial share. At least seven days before any proposal to increase China's voting power is considered, the Treasury Secretary would have to tell Congress whether China is meeting its IMF obligations, keeps open and transparent currency policies, publishes credible trade and financial data, and is not managing its currency against the dollar to gain an unfair trade advantage. If China fails any of these tests, the U.S. representative at the IMF would be required to vote against the increase. The President could waive this by telling Congress it is important to the national interest, and the requirement would end after seven years. As of June 18, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was awaiting a vote by the full House.
for: Supporters say the U.S. should not help give China more say at the IMF unless it follows the fund's rules and stops manipulating its currency to gain a trade edge.
against: Critics say tying U.S. votes to these tests could strain cooperation at the IMF and reduce U.S. flexibility in negotiations, though the bill does let the President waive the requirement.
